'''Michael Patrick Cava''' (13 February 1926 – 29 September 2010) was an American organic chemist and the Ramsay Professor Emeritus of Chemistry at the [[University of Alabama]].

== Biography ==
Cava was born in [[Brooklyn, New York]], on 13 February 1926 to Italian parents. As a child, he tried chemical experiments at home with his friend [[Jerrold Meinwald]]. He graduated from [[Harvard University]] in 1946 and then earned his MS and PhD from the [[University of Michigan]] in 1948 and 1951, respectively. His doctoral supervisor was [[Werner Emmanuel Bachmann]], who died during his studies. He then continued his research with the help of [[André Dreiding]].<ref name="UA">{{cite web|title= About the Cava Lecture Series|url= https://chemistry.ua.edu/department-overview/seminars-and-lectures/about-the-cava-lecture-series/ |website=The University of Abalama|accessdate=15 October 2026}}</ref>

He conducted research as a postdoctoral fellow with [[Robert Burns Woodward]] at Harvard University for two years. He then took up a position as an assistant professor at [[Ohio State University]], where he was promoted to full professor in 1965. In 1965, he transferred to [[Wayne State University]]. He worked at the [[University of Pennsylvania]] from 1969 to 1985. In 1985, he was appointed to the Ramsay Chair of Chemistry at the [[University of Alabama]], where he remained until his retirement in 2004.<ref name="CEN">{{cite web|first= Susan J. |last=Ainsworth|title= Michael P. Cava|website=Chemical & Engineering News|date=29 November 2010|accessdate=15 October 2026| url= https://cen.acs.org/articles/88/i48/Michael-P-Cava.html}}</ref><ref name="UPA"/>

During his career, he served a visiting professor at the [[University of Illinois]] in 1957 and the [[University of California at Santa Barbara]] in 1968. He was also a Raman Visiting professor at the [[University of Madras]] in 1973.<ref name="UA"/>

He was an emeritus member of the [[American Chemical Society]]. He was also a [[Sloan Fellow]] from 1958 to 1962 and a [[Guggenheim Fellow]] from 1984 to 1985. He died on 29 September 2010 in [[Brookline, Massachusetts]], at the age of 84.<ref name="UA"/>

== Research ==
His research focused on synthetic organic chemistry including cyclobutadiene derivatives, biological compounds, [[organic conductor]]s, [[conductive polymer]]s, and nonlinear optical materials.<ref name="CEN"/>

In 1978, he and his collaborators reported the synthesis of [[bis(ethylenedithio)tetrathiafulvalene]] (BEDT-TTF),<ref>{{cite journal|first1=Masao|last1=Mizuno|first2=Anthony F.|last2=Garito|first3=Michael P.|last3=Cava|title='Organic metals': alkylthio substitution effects in tetrathiafulvalene–tetracyanoquinodimethane charge-transfer complexes|journal=Journal of the Chemical Society, Chemical Communications|year=1978|pages=18–19|doi=10.1039/C39780000018}}</ref> whose [[charge transfer complex]]s have yielded the numerous [[organic superconductor]]s.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Mori|first1=Hatsumi|title=Materials Viewpoint of Organic Superconductors|journal=Journal of the Physical Society of Japan|volume=75|issue=5|at=051003|year=2006|doi=10.1143/JPSJ.75.051003|bibcode=2006JPSJ...75e1003M}}</ref>

== Personal ==
He married his first wife, Esther Laden of [[Duluth, Minnesota]], in 1951. An expert in adolescent psychology, she died in 1995. Their son, John, became an architect in [[Portland, Oregon]]. He is survived by his second wife, Armelle Guinard; his son, John; and his granddaughter, Sophie Rose.<ref name="UA"/><ref name="UPA">{{cite web|url= https://almanac.upenn.edu/archive/volumes/v57/n07/obit.html |title=Deaths |accessdate=15 October 2026|website=UPenn Almanac}}</ref>
